newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb army goes to the polls.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb army goes to the polls.

text.p: Bosnian Serb army soldiers on Friday cast their ballots on the eve of elections which organisers say should bring peace and unity to the country but which critics argue will keep it divided.

"I'm afraid this will turn into something totally different from what the world wants," Srecko Maricic, a soldier from a north Bosnian village told Reuters outside the polling station in a schoolhouse in town 30km (18 miles) west of Banja Luka.

It is almost exactly one year ago that NATO bombed Maricic's fellow soldiers, reversing earlier Bosnian Serb Army (BSA) gains which brought them 70 percent of the country and paving the way for the Dayton peace talks in November.
The schoolhouse in Stricici is one of three polling stations opened on Friday morning for the BSA to vote. The other two are in Vlasenica and Kalinovik.

The soldiers will be on guard duty on Saturday to prevent possible violence when some 2.9 million voters from rival and still embittered ethnic communities meet at over 4,000 polling stations across the country.
Some 140,000 people are expected to cross ethnic boundary lines and vote in their home towns, many of them for the first time since they fled or were driven out during the 43-month war.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), in charge of the elections, has traced 19 safe routes for the people to use and won a promise earlier this week by local police chiefs on all three sides that returning refugees will be protected.
Heavily armed NATO forces will be on hand just in case as voters elect cantonal assemblies, separate Moslem-Croat and Serb parliaments, a national House of Representatives and a three-man presidency.

The authors of the Dayton peace accord which ended the Bosnian war last December believe the elections can help reunite the country by forcing former enemies to sit together and cooperate in joint governing bodies.
But the Bosnian Serbs do not agree, despite warnings by international organisers that the ethnic partition of Bosnia is not an option.
"Dayton was forced on us," Bosnian Serb Prime Minister Gojko Klickovic said on Thursday evening just hours before an end to campaigning and an alcohol ban were imposed at midnight.
The ruling Bosnian Serb Democratic Party (SDS) was fined $50,000 earlier this week for openly declaring its ultimate goal was to detach the Serb sector from Bosnia and join it to Serbia.
The Bosnian Serb opposition, mainly from the Bosnian branch of Serbia's ruling Socialist party, favours a more pragmatic nationalism foreseeing cooperation with neighbouring peoples.
But with two opposition blocs ranged against the SDS effectively competing with each other, there is little chance either will win a majority in the 80-seat Bosnian Serb parliament.

Three candidates are going for the post of Bosnian Serb President, which implies control of the Bosnian Serb Army -- incumbent Biljana Plavsic, the Socialist candidate Zivko Radisic and the charismatic mayor of Banja Luka Predrag Radic who heads the Democratic Patriotic Bloc.
